item.title: Atlantic Tropical Weather Outlook
item.description:
047
ABNT20 KNHC 281116
TWOAT

Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
800 AM EDT Mon Sep 28 2026

For the North Atlantic...Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of America:

Active Systems:
The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on Tropical
Depression Fay, located well to the southwest of the Azores.

Central Subtropical Atlantic (AL91):
An area of low pressure located well to the east-northeast of
Bermuda is moving quickly eastward. Recent microwave imagery
suggests the shower and thunderstorm activity is beginning to show
signs of organization, though it is unclear if the system has
developed a well-defined circulation given its fast forward motion.
While environmental conditions are currently only marginally
favorable, this system is now likely to become a tropical depression
or storm over the next day or two as it turns east-southeastward and
slows down over the central Subtropical Atlantic. Environmental
conditions are expected to become unfavorable for further
development later this week.
* Formation chance through 48 hours...high...70 percent.
* Formation chance through 7 days...high...80 percent.

$$
Forecaster Papin

SUMMARY OF 300 PM GMT...1500 UTC...INFORMATION
----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...27.1N 44.6W
ABOUT 1265 MI...2040 KM WSW OF THE AZORES
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...35 MPH...55 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...SSW OR 210 DEGREES AT 9 MPH...15 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...1011 MB...29.86 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 300 PM GMT (1500 UTC), the center of Tropical Depression Fay was 
located near latitude 27.1 North, longitude 44.6 West. The 
depression is moving toward the south-southwest near 9 mph (15 
km/h). A turn to the southwest and then to the west-southwest, along 
with an increase in forward motion, is expected over the next couple 
of days.
 
Maximum sustained winds are near 35 mph (55 km/h) with higher gusts. 
Little change in strength is forecast during the next day or so, and 
Fay is forecast to become a post-tropical cyclone on Tuesday.
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 1011 mb (29.86 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
None.
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
Next complete advisory at 900 PM GMT.
 
$$
Forecaster Kelly

item.title: Tropical Depression Fay Forecast Discussion Number 34
item.description:
Issued at 300 PM GMT Mon Sep 28 2026 
000
WTNT41 KNHC 281439
TCDAT1
 
Tropical Depression Fay Discussion Number  34
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       AL062026
300 PM GMT Mon Sep 28 2026
 
Fay continues to produce bursts of deep convection, mainly to the 
south of the low-level center. A recent ASCAT-B scatterometer pass 
indicated the highest reliable satellite-derived surface winds were 
around 25-30 kt, which is in good agreement with the TAFB subjective 
Dvorak intensity estimate of T2.0/30 kt. Although some of the 
UW-CIMSS objective intensity estimates are higher, the initial 
intensity is held at 30 kt, leaning toward the scatterometer data.
 
The initial motion is estimated to be south-southwestward, or  
210/8 kt. Fay should continue to move south-southwestward to 
southwestward along the southern periphery of a subtropical ridge 
located over the central Atlantic. Track guidance is in fairly good 
agreement on this general motion, with the primary differences being 
in the along-track spread. The latest NHC track forecast is slightly 
faster than the previous advisory and lies near the HCCA 
corrected-consensus aid.
 
Fay has maintained persistent convection near the low-level center 
within a favorable environment over warm sea surface temperatures, 
low vertical wind shear, and abundant mid-level moisture. It is 
possible Fay could regain tropical storm strength. However, this 
favorable environment is expected to be short-lived. Global models 
continue to show the system will struggle to produce deep convection 
in a day or so as it encounters a more stable air mass and 
convergence aloft. The latest NHC intensity forecast is similar to 
the previous one, showing the system dissipating late Tuesday and 
degenerating into a surface trough shortly thereafter.

item.title: Tropical Storm Hanna Forecast Discussion Number 1
item.description:
Issued at 1100 AM AST Mon Sep 28 2026 
000
WTNT43 KNHC 281500
TCDAT3
 
Tropical Storm Hanna Discussion Number   1
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       AL082026
1100 AM AST Mon Sep 28 2026
 
Recent scatterometer data shows that the disturbance that NHC has 
been tracking over the central subtropical Atlantic has acquired a 
well-defined surface circulation and center.  Despite significant 
westerly shear the system has maintained an area of deep convection 
to the east of the center, and the scatterometer data revealed peak 
winds of 35 to 40 kt to the southeast of the center.  As a result 
of this data, the system is being upgraded to 40-kt tropical 
storm Hanna at this time.  

The shear over the tropical storm is expected to remain strong out 
of the west-northwest for the next several days, so little, if any, 
strengthening is anticipated.  In a couple of days, the shear and 
dry mid-level air are likely to cause weakening.  Simulated 
satellite imagery from the global models indicated the deep 
convection is likely to cease in about 60 hours, therefore the NHC 
forecast calls for it to become a remnant low at that time. 

Hanna is moving eastward at about 15 kt.  An eastward to 
east-southeastward motion is forecast during the next 24 hours as 
the system is embedded along the southern side of the mid-latitude 
westerlies. After that time, the westerlies lift northward and the 
steering flow will weaken, causing the system to slow down and turn 
east-northeastward. The NHC track forecast is close to the HCCA and 
GDMI models which are along the southern side of the model envelope.
